opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the core reason is that the problems we're working on are genuinely hard, and they're hard in ways where being wrong can matter a lot. When you're building systems that might become extraordinarily capable, the worst failure mode for an organization is one where people see something concerning, whether it's a safety issue, a strategic mistake, or just a bad decision by leadership, and they don't say it. Or they say it in a softened, filtered way that loses the signal.

Every organization drifts toward telling the people at the top what they want to hear. That's just how human institutions work. Incentives push information upward in a sanitized form, and by the time it reaches decision-makers, the uncomfortable parts have been sanded off. I've seen that happen at other places, and I think it's one of the most dangerous dynamics a company in this field can have.

So I try to push hard in the other direction. I write fairly long, candid documents about how I'm thinking about strategy, about where I'm uncertain, about where I think we might be getting things wrong, and I share them broadly internally. I want people to argue with me. I want the person who thinks our approach to some safety evaluation is flawed to write that up and post it where everyone can see it. If I only hear agreement, that's a sign something is broken, not that we're right.

There's also a trust element. We're asking people to make real tradeoffs. Sometimes we hold back on things commercially because of safety concerns, sometimes we make decisions that are controversial. People can only buy into that if they understand the actual reasoning, not a PR version of it. If the internal story and the real story diverge, you lose people's trust, and you lose their ability to catch your mistakes.

And honestly, at the speed this field is moving, you can't afford slow, filtered information. Things change month to month. The organization has to be able to notice reality quickly and update. Unfiltered communication is basically how a company stays in contact with reality.

r001.rationale: The response discusses filtered information inside organizations, but does not say public audiences may interpret statements in bad faith or that this necessitates defensive corporate communication.

r002.rationale: It says employees need to understand the reasoning to buy into decisions and retain trust in the organization; it does not identify the organization’s trust in employees as enabling unfiltered communication.

r003.rationale: The response says open communication helps the organization catch mistakes and stay in contact with reality, but does not claim employees collectively achieve more than the sum of their individual contributions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple observation: the most dangerous thing in an organization is a gap between what people actually believe and what gets said out loud. And that gap tends to widen quietly. Nobody decides to stop telling the truth. It's just that, one meeting at a time, people learn that the honest version of something costs them a little more than the polished version, and so they start reaching for the polished version by default.

For most companies that's a tax on efficiency. For us, I think it's existential. The whole premise of Anthropic is that we're trying to make a technology that we genuinely think could be dangerous, and do it carefully. That only works if, when someone on a safety team sees something concerning, or someone on a research team thinks a direction isn't going to pan out, or someone thinks I'm wrong about a strategic call, the information actually travels. If it gets softened three times on the way up, by the time it reaches the people making decisions it's not information anymore. It's just reassurance.

And there's a second piece, which is trust. We ask people to extend a lot of trust to the organization. We tell them we're going to make hard calls that are sometimes uncomfortable, that we're not going to do certain things that would be commercially attractive. The only way that kind of trust holds up is if people can see the reasoning, including the parts where we're uncertain or where we've changed our minds. I'd much rather someone read a memo and say "I disagree with this" than have them read a sanitized version and quietly conclude that leadership either isn't thinking hard about it or isn't being straight with them.

I'll admit it has real costs. Things get said that are blunt, things leak occasionally, and you have to be willing to be wrong in front of a lot of people. But I think the alternative, where everyone's performing confidence and the real conversations happen in DMs, is much worse. In the thing we're doing, the failure mode isn't that someone's feelings get hurt. It's that the organization believes something false about itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses internal honesty and the risks of softened information, but does not mention public audiences misinterpreting statements or defensive corporate communication.

r002.rationale: It says transparency helps employees trust the organization; it does not say that the organization’s trust in employees permits unfiltered communication.

r003.rationale: It describes information reaching decision-makers and organizational trust, but does not claim that unfiltered communication lets employees achieve more collectively than their individual contributions.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest reason is that, as an organization grows, it becomes increasingly easy for leadership to lose touch with what’s actually happening. People tell you what they think you want to hear. Bad news gets softened as it travels up the chain. You can have a company full of smart people and still make terrible decisions because the relevant information never reaches the people making them.

That’s especially concerning when you’re working on AI, where there’s so much uncertainty. We need people to be able to say, “I think this assumption is wrong,” or “This result doesn’t support the story we’re telling,” including when the person telling that story is me. If disagreement feels costly, you lose one of your most important mechanisms for correcting mistakes.

And it has to go both ways. You can’t ask people to be candid while giving them a carefully managed version of your own thinking. You have to explain why you’re making decisions, what you’re uncertain about, and where there are real tradeoffs. That gives people the context to exercise judgment rather than just follow instructions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses leadership losing access to accurate internal information, but does not mention public audiences or defensive corporate communication.

r002.rationale: It calls for candid internal disagreement and leaders sharing their thinking, but does not identify employee trust as the condition that permits unfiltered communication.

r003.rationale: It says candid communication helps correct mistakes and improve decisions, but does not claim employees achieve more collectively than the sum of individual contributions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central reason is that, as an organization grows, it gets harder to know what’s actually happening. People have incentives to tell you what you want to hear, to make their project look good, or simply to avoid an uncomfortable conversation. You can end up with very smart people collectively making bad decisions because the relevant information never reaches the right place.

And we’re working on something where there’s a lot of uncertainty. We need people to be able to say, “I think this assumption is wrong,” or “This result worries me,” including when that’s inconvenient or cuts against something leadership believes. If people don’t feel comfortable doing that, we lose a major mechanism for correcting our mistakes.

That doesn’t mean every discussion has to involve everyone, or that being abrasive is somehow a virtue. It means you should be able to raise a substantive concern without having to calculate whether it’s politically safe. I want the information that changes my mind to reach me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses internal information flow and organizational incentives, but says nothing about public audiences interpreting statements in bad faith or defensive corporate communication.

r002.rationale: It encourages employees to raise concerns without fear of political consequences, but does not identify trust in employees as what permits entirely unfiltered communication.

r003.rationale: It says open communication helps correct mistakes, but does not claim that employees collectively achieve more than the sum of their individual contributions.
